title: Sandcastles v. the Himalayas: On Weak and Strong Boundaries
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Writing during a stretch of remote and hybrid instruction saturated with boundary-setting advice, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that most teacher boundaries fail because they're merely stated rather than structurally enforced, what he calls 'sandcastle boundaries.' He proposes 'Himalayan boundaries' instead: constraints built into the environment itself, immovable enough that willpower and good intentions become unnecessary. His central example is email; rather than telling people when you'll respond, delete the email app from your phone entirely and have a spouse password-protect app downloads, so the boundary can't be casually undone in a weak moment. For the harder problem of not bringing work home, he recommends recruiting a trusted friend or spouse as an external accountability check who is explicitly asked to challenge you when you break your stated work hours. The piece links directly back to his 'workload-pressure paradox' concept, framing durable boundaries as the necessary first step toward the kind of expertise that lets teachers focus, satisfice, and skip non-essential work rather than burning out under an ever-expanding workload.
points: Stuart distinguishes 'sandcastle boundaries' (stated intentions with no enforcement mechanism, like telling people when you'll check email) from 'Himalayan boundaries' (structural changes that remove the option to transgress, like deleting email apps from your phone).

His email example operationalizes OHIO (Only Handle It Once) as the enforcement mechanism inside a Himalayan boundary: checking once daily and structurally blocking after-hours access rather than relying on willpower.

For the harder 'not bringing work home' boundary, Stuart recommends recruiting a spouse or trusted friend as an external accountability check, explicitly asking them to challenge you when the boundary is broken rather than trusting self-monitoring alone.

The piece explicitly ties boundary-setting to his separately-named 'workload-pressure paradox,' positioning boundaries as the entry point for building the expertise needed to satisfice and skip non-essential work.
quotes: The trouble is that a lot of this boundary talk ends up being just that: talk. We talk about them, we share them with a friend, we say we'll do them, we make sure students or parents know about them… and then we transgress them.
In other words, we make sandcastle boundaries. They're pretty — but wimpy, too. A bit of self-indulgence rain, a rogue crashing wave of workload, and whoosh — bye bye, boundaries.

What we need are Himalayan boundaries: the kinds of things that life can't move so easily, that require Herculean effort to overcome. South Asian history is in some ways the story of how a boundary like the Himalayas made possible the development of a unique set of human cultures.

Setting a rule for yourself that you'll check email only one time per day, and when you do, you'll OHIO — only handle it once. Deleting email apps off your smartphone and then asking your friend or spouse to password-protect app downloading on your phone.

I've told them that limiting my work to these times is a most serious matter to me — it's what's keeping me from realizing my potential as an educator, from getting the breakthroughs that I need for "more learning, less stress.

In all of this, what you and I want is to look back on well-shaped careers and well-shaped lives. But the default modern life isn't one that works like that: instead it's frantic, frenetic, self-indulgent, crazed.
So: sandcastles won't work for what we're after. It's time to find some mountains.
